analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income tax with a flat 17% tax on wages and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill attracted no cosponsors, was never taken up by the Finance Committee, and died there when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the current income tax and replaced it with one flat 17% rate. But it would only tax money from paychecks, pensions, and unemployment checks — income from investments like capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents would owe no federal income tax at all. It would also wipe out the estate tax on inherited fortunes, repeal every tax credit (including the earned income and child tax credits that boost working families' pay), strip out the rules that keep employer retirement plans fair to rank-and-file workers, and let companies pull money out of overfunded pensions with only a modest tax. It never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest winners would be wealthy households: income from capital gains, dividends, interest, and rent would be untaxed entirely, and the estate tax on multi-million-dollar inheritances would disappear. High-earning employees would gain from the single 17% rate on their wages, and business owners would gain from a 17% business tax replacing the corporate income tax and the alternative minimum tax. Employers with overfunded pensions could pull those surpluses out paying only ordinary income tax instead of the current 20-50% excise penalty, and executives would gain from pension plans no longer required to cover or benefit rank-and-file workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: It replaced the current marginal income tax rates with a single 17% rate, and only on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above a standard deduction of $28,140 for couples — meaning interest, dividends, capital gains, and rent income would owe no federal income tax at all.
It repealed the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely, ending federal taxation of very large inherited fortunes.

It replaced the corporate income tax with a 17% tax on business income and repealed the alternative minimum tax, and let employers withdraw excess pension assets paying only normal income tax instead of the current excise penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Workers paid by paycheck would bear most of the tax load, since wages are the only major income the bill taxes — a wage earner at the standard deduction threshold would pay 17 cents on every dollar above it while an investor living off capital gains would owe nothing. Working families would lose the earned income tax credit, child tax credit, mortgage interest deduction, and charitable deduction. Government and nonprofit employees would see their employers pay a new 17% tax on their benefits, and workers' retirement savings would lose protections: plans could favor executives, contribution limits would end, and early-withdrawal penalties would vanish.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers paid by paycheck and their families

drawbacks.text: Repealing all income tax credits would have eliminated the earned income tax credit and the child tax credit, which lift millions of working families' take-home pay, and repealing all income tax provisions would have ended deductions like mortgage interest and charitable giving.

The repeal of pension nondiscrimination and coverage rules would have allowed 401(k) and pension plans to be designed for the benefit of executives, removing the rules that require plans to cover ordinary employees.

Ending the excise tax on employer reversions would have let companies withdraw surplus assets from their pension funds — money that currently faces a 20-50% penalty — leaving only ordinary income tax, which pension experts warned could underfund worker plans.

Taxing only cash wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation means people living primarily on capital income would pay almost nothing, and the bill included no analysis of how the revenue lost from repealing income, estate, and gift taxes would be replaced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's selling point — a single 17% rate and a tax code simple enough to file on a postcard — was real, but its design achieved simplicity by moving the tax burden off unearned income and onto wages. Repealing every tax credit would have pulled the earned income and child tax credits out from under millions of working families, and repealing the estate tax would have eliminated the only federal tax on very large inherited fortunes. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill traded simplification for a large upward redistribution, and that its projected growth was asserted in the title rather than demonstrated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 29, 2013 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken: the Finance Committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor, even among its sponsor's fellow Republicans.
The bill died in committee when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working families kept the existing tax code, including the earned income and child tax credits, and the estate tax stayed on large inherited fortunes — the bill's principal beneficiaries got nothing because it never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families kept the existing tax code

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 29, 2013; it was his first flat tax proposal of the new Congress and it was referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 29, 2013 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never became a partisan fight: Shelby introduced it alone and did not attract a single cosponsor from either party, and no chamber ever considered it.

industries.note: Capital gains, dividends, interest, and rent would owe no federal income tax under the bill's wage-only taxable income definition, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would be repealed outright. Estates over $5 million per person currently face a 40% tax on the excess, so this is the single largest giveaway in the bill.

A 17% tax on business income replaces the corporate tax, employers could withdraw excess pension assets paying only ordinary income tax instead of a 20-50% excise penalty, and pension rules restricting plan design for executives would be repealed. Employers of government and nonprofit workers would face a new 17% tax on their employees' fringe benefits.

industries.industry: State and local governments and tax-exempt organizations
industries.note: The bill would impose a 17% employer-paid tax on the value of fringe benefits — like health insurance — provided to government and nonprofit employees, a cost those employers currently do not bear.

industries.industry: Retirement plan participants and the financial services industry
industries.note: Repealing contribution limits and early-withdrawal penalties would loosen rules for savers and the firms managing retirement money, but repealing nondiscrimination rules would let plans be skewed toward executives, and letting employers pull surplus assets out of pensions puts worker retirement security at risk.
